tip: 은/는 sets the topic — 'as for X': 저는 커피를 좋아해요 (jeo-neun keopi-reul joahaeyo).
이/가 marks the subject — 가 after a vowel, 이 after a consonant: 친구가 와요 (chingu-ga wayo).
One present tense does both English presents: 버스가 와요 (beoseu-ga wayo) means 'the bus comes' or 'the bus is coming' – no separate -ing form needed.
No verb for 'have' here – 시간이 없어요 (sigan-i eopseoyo) is literally 'time doesn't exist'. The thing you lack is the subject, so it takes 이 (i).
에 marks a destination or a time: 학교에 가요 (hakgyo-e gayo = I go to school).

english: I drink coffee at a cafe.
tip: 에서 marks where an action happens: 카페에서 마셔요 (kape-eseo masyeoyo = I drink at a cafe).
The verb always comes last: 식당에서 밥을 먹어요 (sikdang-eseo bab-eul meogeoyo) runs 'restaurant-at rice eat'. Place and object first, action at the end.
도 (do = too) replaces the object marker instead of stacking on it: 빵도 사요 (ppang-do sayo), never 빵을도 (ppang-eul-do). It attaches straight to the noun it covers.
안 goes right before the verb: 안 먹어요 (an meogeoyo = I don't eat).
With 하다 (hada) verbs, 안 (an = not) slips between the noun and the verb: 공부 안 해요 (gongbu an haeyo) – not 안 공부해요 (an gongbuhaeyo).
못 = can't, 안 = don't: 못 가요 (mot gayo = I can't go).
찾아요 means both 'look for' and 'find': 우산을 찾아요 (usan-eul chajayo = I look for my umbrella).
입어요 (ibeoyo = wear) is only for clothes on the body: 옷을 입어요 (os-eul ibeoyo). Shoes take 신어요 (sineoyo), hats and glasses 써요 (sseoyo) – one English 'wear', three Korean verbs.
English gets ON the bus; Korean rides it as a direct object: 버스를 타요 (beoseureul tayo) uses 를 (reul), no word for 'on' at all.
You ride transport as a direct object: 지하철을 타요 (jihacheor-eul tayo = I take the subway). 타요 (tayo) covers buses, taxis and trains too – no 'on' or 'in' needed.

english: My younger sibling reads the newspaper.
tip: 봐요 covers watching and casual reading: 신문을 봐요 (sinmun-eul bwayo = I read the paper).
언니 (eonni) = a woman's older sister; men say 누나 (nuna).
Question words sit where the answer would: 화장실이 어디에 있어요? (hwajangsir-i eodi-e isseoyo?) is literally 'the bathroom is where?' – no need to move 어디 (eodi) to the front.

english: What are you buying at the store?
tip: In speech 을/를 often drops: 뭐를 사요? → 뭐 사요? (mwo sayo? = what are you buying?)
Yes-no questions keep statement word order – no 'do', no flipping: 맥주를 마셔요? (maekju-reul masyeoyo?) is just 'you drink beer' said with rising tone.

english: I use a computer at work.
tip: 써요 means 'write' and also 'use': 컴퓨터를 써요 (keompyuteo-reul sseoyo = I use a computer).
필요해요 'need' takes 이/가, not 을/를: 커피가 필요해요 (keopi-ga piryohaeyo = I need coffee).
뭐 (mwo = what) sits right where the answer would go – no inversion: 지금 뭐 해요? (jigeum mwo haeyo?) is literally 'now what do?'
A Korean question is just a statement with rising tone – no 'do', no word flip: 먹어요 (meogeoyo) covers both 'I eat' and 'are you eating?'.
어디 (eodi = where) usually drops its particle in speech: 어디 가요? (eodi gayo? = where are you going?)
English drags 'where' to the front; Korean leaves it next to the verb: 화장실이 어디예요? (hwajangsil-i eodi-yeyo?) is literally 'the bathroom is where?'.
Korean rarely says 'he' or 'she' – you say 그 사람 (geu saram = that person) instead, even where English would use a pronoun.
No 'for' after waiting: 기다려요 (gidaryeoyo = wait) takes a direct object, so it's 누구를 (nugu-reul = whom), not 'for whom'.
랑 (rang) is the casual spoken 'with', glued to the end of its noun: 누구랑 (nugu-rang = with whom). Formal or written Korean uses 와/과 (wa/gwa) instead.
Name + 씨 (ssi) stays polite even when talking ABOUT someone, not just to them: 민수 씨가 누구예요? (Minsu ssi-ga nuguyeyo? = who is Minsu?)
